newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - NAPM, payrolls data, FOMC on tap.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - NAPM, payrolls data, FOMC on tap.

text.p: The bond market may have an eventful week ahead, with participants prepared to digest some of the earliest data on first-quarter U.S. growth as central bank policy makers meet to set growth targets for year.

Few analysts expect the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) would vote to tighten policy, but such a move could not be dismissed out of hand. The FOMC meets on Tuesday and Wednesday, and, any change would not be announced until Wednesday.
Also, President Clinton unveils his budget on Thursday.
The week starts off Monday with the release of personal income and consumption data followed shortly by the National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) January index.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has said he viewed NAPM as a forward-looking indicator, and, as such one he paid attention to when trying to gauge strength in the manufacturing sector. Construction spending also will be released on Monday.

On Friday the all-important nonfarm payrolls report was scheduled for release and in between factory orders were slated for Thursday release and leading economic indicators on Tuesday. Car sales were set throughout the week.

"We've entered a period of time where the data should begin to show signs the economy is slowing. Growth has been above its trend line and interest rates have risen as a result," said Mickey Levy, chief financial economist at Nationsbanc Capital Markets Inc.
He said NAPM could be a touch weaker and that as the economy slows, interest rates should recede but the labor market was likely to remain tight.
"That makes the wage number in the payrolls report the biggest issue. Greenspan has all but said that's what he's focused on," Levy said.

"The whole market's attitude seems to have changed in the last few days. Players are just relieved that the Fed doesn't seem poised to raise rates," said Mitchell Held, chief economist at Smith Barney & Co.

Held saw payrolls rising by only 150,000 in January and no change in average hourly earnings, factors favorable for the current inflation watch. Outside of energy, inflation seemed contained as producers can't pass along costs to consumers.
Held also said a conciliatory tone continued to mark budget talks and that this long after an election "both sides are saying the right thing, and that's good."

Dan Seto, economist at Nikko Securities International Inc., said he was skeptical the bond market could advance much next week and that the gains seen in Friday's trading session were probably based on an improved deflator number in the GDP, one people will come to realize was aided by export prices.
"I expect a pullback. The market feels comfortable with the inflation picture right now, but current conditions are still too strong to warrant that confidence," Seto said.
Consequently, the prices paid component of the NAPM will be more important than the overall index, which has been in a mid-50s range and should stay there, Seto said.

"Whereas in 1996 people (at the Fed) looked for all kinds of reasons not to raise rates, the talk now has taken on a preemptive tone. They're reviving the kind of language that signals a shift in the approach to policy," Seto said.

Late Friday, the two-year note was 99-29/32, up 5/32, to yield 5.93 percent. The 10-year was up 18/32 at 99-30/32 to yield 6.51 percent. The 30-year bond was up 30/32 at 96-8/32 to yield 6.79 percent.
